```{r}
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
    library(base64enc)
    library(dplyr)
    library(knitr)
    library(purrr)
    library(readxl)
})

# Load results
output_dir <- "output/so_prediction_rev"
xlsx_path <- file.path(output_dir, "results.xlsx")
sheets <- excel_sheets(xlsx_path)
sheets <- setNames(sheets, gsub(" ", "_", tolower(sheets)))
results <- map(sheets, read_excel, path = xlsx_path)

# Analysis settings not exported to the results workbook
n_trees <- 1000L
n_metric_bootstrap <- 10000L
n_selection_bootstrap <- 2000L

# Formatting helpers
fmt <- function(x, digits = 3) {
    formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
}

fmt_integer <- function(x) {
    formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
}

format_power_of_ten <- function(x) {
    exponent <- formatC(log10(x), format = "f", digits = 0)
    paste0("\\\\(10^{", exponent, "}\\\\)")
}

download_button <- function(path, filename, label, mime) {
    stopifnot(file.exists(path), length(filename) == 1L, length(label) == 1L)
    encoded_file <- base64encode(path)
    sprintf(
        paste0(
            '<a href="data:%s;base64,%s" download="%s" ',
            'class="btn btn-primary" role="button">',
            '<i class="bi bi-download" aria-hidden="true"></i> %s</a>'
        ),
        mime,
        encoded_file,
        filename,
        label
    )
}

# Result lookup helpers
metric_value <- function(model, class, metric, component = "Estimate") {
    column <- paste(component, model, sep = "_")
    row <- results$performance_metrics |>
        filter(Class == class, Metric == metric)
    stopifnot(nrow(row) == 1L, column %in% names(row))
    row[[column]]
}

difference_value <- function(class, metric, component) {
    row <- results$paired_model_differences |>
        filter(Class == class, Metric == metric)
    stopifnot(nrow(row) == 1L, component %in% names(row))
    row[[component]]
}

class_count <- function(class) {
    sum(results$predictions$observed == class)
}

confusion_count <- function(model, observed, predicted) {
    sheet <- results[[paste0(model, "_confusion_matrix")]]
    row <- sheet |>
        filter(
            .data$observed == .env$observed,
            .data$predicted == .env$predicted
        )
    stopifnot(nrow(row) == 1L)
    row$Freq
}

confusion_display <- function(model) {
    sheet <- results[[paste0(model, "_confusion_matrix")]]
    matrix <- xtabs(Freq ~ observed + predicted, data = sheet)
    data.frame(
        Observed = rownames(matrix),
        as.data.frame.matrix(matrix),
        row.names = NULL,
        check.names = FALSE
    )
}

format_metric_ci <- function(model, class, metric) {
    paste0(
        fmt(metric_value(model, class, metric, "Estimate")),
        " (95% CI ",
        fmt(metric_value(model, class, metric, "Lower")),
        "–",
        fmt(metric_value(model, class, metric, "Upper")),
        ")"
    )
}

format_difference_ci <- function(class, metric) {
    paste0(
        fmt(difference_value(class, metric, "Difference_RF_minus_LASSO")),
        ", ",
        fmt(difference_value(class, metric, "Lower")),
        "–",
        fmt(difference_value(class, metric, "Upper"))
    )
}

n_patients <- length(unique(results$predictions$pid))
n_observations <- nrow(results$predictions)
n_predictors <- length(unique(results$rf_variable_importance$predictor))

class_counts <- setNames(
    map_int(c("exertion", "relative.humidity", "temperature"), class_count),
    c("exertion", "relative_humidity", "temperature")
)

n_correct_rf <- sum(
    results$predictions$observed == results$predictions$predicted_rf
)
n_correct_lasso <- sum(
    results$predictions$observed == results$predictions$predicted_lasso
)
stopifnot(identical(
    results$predictions$predicted_rf,
    results$predictions$predicted_lasso
))
n_temperature_as_humidity_rf <- confusion_count(
    "rf", "temperature", "relative.humidity"
)

rf_mtry_min <- min(results$rf_tuning_profile$mtry)
rf_mtry_max <- max(results$rf_tuning_profile$mtry)
rf_accuracy_min <- min(results$rf_tuning_profile$Accuracy)
rf_accuracy_max <- max(results$rf_tuning_profile$Accuracy)
rf_best_mtry <- results$rf_tuning_profile$mtry[
    results$rf_tuning_profile$Accuracy == rf_accuracy_max
]

lasso_alpha <- unique(results$lasso_tuning_profile$alpha)
n_lambda <- nrow(results$lasso_tuning_profile)
lambda_min <- min(results$lasso_tuning_profile$lambda)
lambda_max <- max(results$lasso_tuning_profile$lambda)

performance_comparison <- data.frame(
    Metric = c(
        "Accuracy",
        "Multiclass Brier score",
        "Multiclass log loss",
        "Macro AUC"
    ),
    RF = c(
        fmt(metric_value("rf", "Overall", "Accuracy")),
        fmt(metric_value("rf", "Overall", "Multiclass Brier Score")),
        fmt(metric_value("rf", "Overall", "Multiclass Log Loss")),
        fmt(metric_value("rf", "Macro Average", "AUC"))
    ),
    LASSO = c(
        fmt(metric_value("lasso", "Overall", "Accuracy")),
        fmt(metric_value("lasso", "Overall", "Multiclass Brier Score")),
        fmt(metric_value("lasso", "Overall", "Multiclass Log Loss")),
        fmt(metric_value("lasso", "Macro Average", "AUC"))
    ),
    `RF − LASSO, 95% CI` = c(
        format_difference_ci("Overall", "Accuracy"),
        format_difference_ci("Overall", "Multiclass Brier Score"),
        format_difference_ci("Overall", "Multiclass Log Loss"),
        format_difference_ci("Macro Average", "AUC")
    ),
    check.names = FALSE
)

stability_results <- results$nogueira_stability_index |>
    left_join(results$jaccard_overlap, by = "Class") |>
    transmute(
        Class = recode(
            Class,
            exertion = "Exertion",
            relative.humidity = "Relative humidity",
            temperature = "Temperature"
        ),
        `RF stability` = fmt(RF_Stability),
        `LASSO stability` = fmt(LASSO_Stability),
        `RF–LASSO Jaccard overlap (95% CI)` = paste0(
            fmt(Estimate), " (", fmt(Lower), "–", fmt(Upper), ")"
        )
    )

```

This document addresses only the comments that N. Brasier has flagged as
requiring attention from biostatisticians.

# Answers to comments

## Comment 1

> The handling of within subject correlation in the Random Forest analysis has
> not been corrected. The authors continue to rely on an ad hoc subsampling
> approach (selecting one visit per subject, repeated three times) rather than
> using subject level blocked cross validation or mixed effects models. This
> approach discards a large portion of the available data and artificially
> inflates variance estimates. The authors did not justify why this method is
> preferable to standard alternatives, nor did they provide a sensitivity
> analysis to show that the results are robust to the choice of subsampling. As
> a result, the reported accuracy (i.e., 94.7%) may be overoptimistic and not
> generalizable.

### Answer to comment 1

We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We replaced the previous ad
hoc procedure, in which the visits from each participant were randomly
allocated among three separate datasets and only one visit per participant was
used in each analysis, with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV).

The revised analysis includes all `r n_observations` eligible visits from
`r n_patients` participants. We defined `r n_patients` validation folds, each
containing all observations from one participant. In every fold, the model is
trained using observations from the other `r n_patients - 1` participants and
evaluated on all available visits from the held-out participant. Consequently,
observations from the same participant can never occur simultaneously in the
training and validation datasets. Every eligible visit contributes once to the
collection of held-out predictions.

Missing values are now mean-imputed separately within each training fold
through the preprocessing recipe, thereby avoiding information leakage from the
held-out participant.

We chose subject-blocked cross-validation because the intended prediction
setting concerns generalization to participants who were not represented during
model training. Mixed-effects models address within-participant dependence
under a different modelling framework, whereas subject-blocked validation
directly evaluates this out-of-participant prediction objective.

Uncertainty intervals are also calculated at the participant level. The
`r fmt_integer(n_metric_bootstrap)` bootstrap samples resample participant
identifiers rather than individual visits, and all observations belonging to a
sampled participant are included together. This preserves the
within-participant structure in the calculation of confidence intervals.

Using the revised LOSO predictions, the RF correctly classified
`r n_correct_rf` of `r n_observations` visits, corresponding to an overall
accuracy of `r format_metric_ci("rf", "Overall", "Accuracy")` using the
participant bootstrap. This estimate replaces the previously reported accuracy
of 94.7%.

We nevertheless acknowledge that the sample consists of only `r n_patients`
participants. Furthermore, hyperparameter selection and performance estimation
use the same LOSO resampling (not nested cross-validation) so the estimate may
retain some tuning-selection optimism. The RF tuning surface was nearly flat,
with LOSO accuracy ranging only from `r fmt(rf_accuracy_min)` to
`r fmt(rf_accuracy_max)` across `mtry` = `r rf_mtry_min`,…, `r rf_mtry_max`,
which suggests that this source of optimism is limited but cannot be excluded.

## Comment 2

> The essential classification performance metrics are missing. The manuscript
> reports only overall accuracy with a wide confidence interval. No per class
> precision, recall, F1 scores, confusion matrix, or ROC curves or multiclass
> equivalents are provided. These are necessary to evaluate whether the high
> accuracy is driven by a single class, to assess class imbalance effects, and
> to understand the model’s calibration. The authors declined to include these
> metrics, stating that “they are beyond the scope of this explorative work.” I
> disagree; for a study that centers on a classification model, these are basic
> reporting standards. Furthermore, hyperparameter tuning details (grid search
> range, selection criteria, class weights) are absent as well, the authors
> only cite the caret package defaults, which is insufficient for
> reproducibility.

### Answer to comment 2

We agree and have substantially expanded the reporting of classification
performance. All metrics are calculated exclusively from the held-out LOSO
predictions rather than from predictions on the data used to fit the final
model.

For both RF and LASSO, the revised analysis now reports:

- Confusion matrices
- Overall accuracy
- Class-specific recall/sensitivity
- Specificity
- Precision/positive predictive value
- Negative predictive value
- F1 score
- Balanced accuracy
- One-versus-rest AUC
- Class-specific Brier score and log loss
- Multiclass Brier score and multiclass log loss
- Macro averages of all class-specific metrics
- Participant-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals

The three classes were nearly perfectly balanced: `r class_counts["exertion"]`
exertion, `r class_counts["relative_humidity"]` relative-humidity, and
`r class_counts["temperature"]` temperature observations. No class weights were
therefore applied; all observations received equal weight.

For the RF, the confusion matrix showed perfect classification of exertion and
relative-humidity observations. `r n_temperature_as_humidity_rf` of the
`r class_counts["temperature"]` temperature observations were classified as
relative humidity. The resulting class-specific sensitivities were:

- Exertion: `r fmt(metric_value("rf", "Class: exertion", "Sensitivity"))`
- Relative humidity:
  `r fmt(metric_value("rf", "Class: relative.humidity", "Sensitivity"))`
- Temperature:
  `r format_metric_ci("rf", "Class: temperature", "Sensitivity")`

The macro-averaged F1 score was
`r format_metric_ci("rf", "Macro Average", "F1")`, macro balanced accuracy was
`r format_metric_ci("rf", "Macro Average", "Balanced Accuracy")`, and macro
one-versus-rest AUC was
`r format_metric_ci("rf", "Macro Average", "AUC")`.

Probability-based metrics were added because accuracy and ROC discrimination
alone do not evaluate the quality of predicted probabilities. The RF multiclass
Brier score was
`r format_metric_ci("rf", "Overall", "Multiclass Brier Score")`, and its
multiclass log loss was
`r format_metric_ci("rf", "Overall", "Multiclass Log Loss")`.

We also made hyperparameter tuning fully explicit:

- RF used `r fmt_integer(n_trees)` trees and evaluated
  `mtry` = `r rf_mtry_min`,…, `r rf_mtry_max`.
- Multinomial LASSO used `alpha` = `r lasso_alpha` and evaluated
  `r n_lambda` logarithmically spaced lambda values between
  `r format_power_of_ten(lambda_min)` and
  `r format_power_of_ten(lambda_max)`.

- Both hyperparameters were selected by maximizing mean LOSO accuracy.
- Both models used the identical subject-level folds.
- Missing-value imputation was performed within each training fold.
- Numeric predictors were standardized for LASSO but not RF.

We report one-versus-rest AUCs rather than ROC plots. Given only
`r n_observations` observations and near-perfect separation, ROC curves would
contain relatively little additional information. The AUCs, their confidence
intervals, and the proper probability scoring rules provide the corresponding
quantitative assessment. We do not interpret the Brier score and log loss as a
complete calibration analysis; a reliable calibration curve or calibration
slope would require a substantially larger validation sample.

## Comment 3

> Authors declined to provide a simpler baseline model, e.g., logistic
> regression or LASSO, to demonstrate that the RF’s complexity is warranted and
> that overfitting is not a serious concern. Given the small sample size (n=20)
> and the large number of predictors (55), the risk of overfitting could be
> substantial. The authors added a brief cautionary statement about overfitting
> in the discussion, but they did not perform any empirical check, e.g.,
> permutation importance with uncertainty, or a comparison with a regularized
> model. Without such analyses, the claimed feature importance rankings remain
> unvalidated, in my opinion.

### Answer to comment 3

We agree that comparison with a simpler regularized model is important given
the combination of `r n_patients` participants and `r n_predictors` candidate
predictors. We therefore added a multinomial LASSO logistic-regression model as
a baseline.

The RF and LASSO models use:

- The same observations and predictors
- The same fold-specific imputation
- The same `r n_patients` subject-level LOSO folds
- The same held-out observations for performance assessment
- The same participant-level bootstrap samples for confidence intervals and
  paired comparisons

Numeric predictors are standardized for LASSO because the L1 penalty depends on
predictor scale. RF does not require this normalization.

The RF and LASSO produced exactly the same hard classifications: RF correctly
classified `r n_correct_rf` and LASSO correctly classified `r n_correct_lasso`
of `r n_observations` observations, and both had an accuracy of
`r format_metric_ci("rf", "Overall", "Accuracy")`. Consequently, their
class-specific precision, recall, F1 scores, and balanced accuracies were also
identical.

Their probability-based performance was likewise similar:

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(performance_comparison, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Thus, the revised analysis does not demonstrate a meaningful predictive
advantage for RF over the simpler LASSO model. _The manuscript should state
this explicitly rather than arguing that RF complexity is warranted by superior
predictive performance._

We also evaluated uncertainty in variable selection by performing
`r fmt_integer(n_selection_bootstrap)` participant-level bootstrap resamples.
RF used the previously selected `mtry` without retuning, and LASSO used the
selected lambda. For each class, RF’s top $k$ predictors were compared with the
$k$ nonzero LASSO coefficients, making the selected-set sizes comparable.

The revised analysis reports:

- RF predictor-selection frequencies
- LASSO selection frequencies
- Paired differences in selection frequency with percentile intervals
- Jaccard overlap between RF and LASSO selections
- The Nogueira feature-selection stability index (@nogueira2018stability)

The stability results were moderate rather than uniformly high:

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(stability_results, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

These results indicate strong agreement for the temperature predictors in the
original fit but limited agreement for exertion and relative humidity, with
wide bootstrap uncertainty. _We have therefore tempered the interpretation of
individual feature rankings and now present them as exploratory findings
requiring validation in a larger independent sample._

## Comment 4

Several reproducibility issues persist throughout the entire manuscript. The
handling of core body temperature artefacts (ingestion to peak) is mentioned
but not systematically described, nor did they provide the rule for outlier
exclusion or imputation. The exertion intensity (1 W/kg) was not adjusted for
individual fitness, and no sensitivity analysis stratified by VO₂max was
performed. The authors also argued that RF handles interactions, but this does
not account for confounding by fitness level. These omissions surely weaken the
confidence in reported results.

# Results of the revised analysis

The following tables contain the complete results generated by the revised
analysis. Estimates of predictive performance are based on the held-out LOSO
predictions. Confidence intervals and paired model comparisons use
participant-level bootstrap resampling.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
fig3_path <- file.path(output_dir, "figure3.pdf")
fig3_preview_path <- file.path(output_dir, "figure3.png")
code_path <- "code/so_prediction_rev.R"
buttons <- c(
    download_button(
        xlsx_path,
        "results.xlsx",
        "Download all tables (XLSX)",
        "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet"
    ),
    download_button(
        fig3_path,
        "figure3.pdf",
        "Download Figure 3 (PDF)",
        "application/pdf"
    ),
    download_button(
        code_path,
        "so_prediction_rev.R",
        "Download analysis code (R)",
        "text/plain;charset=utf-8"
    )
)
cat(
    '<div class="d-flex flex-wrap gap-2 mb-4">',
    paste(buttons, collapse = "\n"),
    "</div>"
)
```

## Model predictions

The table contains one held-out prediction from each model for every eligible
visit, together with the corresponding class probabilities.

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(results$predictions, digits = 3)
```

## Predictive performance

The table reports point estimates and participant-bootstrap 95% confidence
intervals for RF and LASSO. Class-specific results use a one-versus-rest
definition, and macro averages assign equal weight to each class.

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(results$performance_metrics, digits = 4)
```

### Paired model comparisons

Differences are calculated as RF minus LASSO using the same held-out
observations and the same bootstrap samples. Positive values favour RF for
metrics where larger values are preferable; negative values favour RF for the
Brier score and log loss.

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(results$paired_model_differences, digits = 4)
```

## Variable importance

RF importance is the unscaled, class-specific permutation importance. LASSO
importance is the absolute standardized coefficient; the coefficient column
retains its direction, and `selected` indicates whether it is nonzero.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Random Forest

```{r}

```

## Variable-selection stability

Selection frequencies are based on participant-level bootstrap resamples. For
each class, the RF selected set contains the same number of predictors as the
nonzero LASSO set in the original fit. The paired difference is RF minus LASSO.

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(results$selection_frequencies, digits = 3)
```
